title: What is canonical theology?
summary: In Christian canonical theology, the Bible is read as a connected collection whose later writings interpret and draw on earlier Scripture. The passages cited here show that practice, while still calling readers to attend to each text's own words and setting.
historical_context: The cited passages are New Testament texts that interpret earlier Scripture. They illustrate canonical reading, but this entry does not document how or when the biblical books were collected into a canon.
canonical_context: The New Testament examples in this entry show several ways earlier Scripture remains active in later writings. In Luke 24, Jesus interprets Moses and the Prophets and speaks of the Psalms in relation to his death and resurrection. Matthew 5 presents his mission in relation to the Law and the Prophets; Romans 15 says earlier writings give readers endurance and hope; and 2 Timothy 3 describes Scripture as instruction that equips its readers. These passages model connected reading, but they do not make every text say the same thing.
literary_context: The cited texts make different kinds of connections. Luke 24 tells a story of interpretation after the resurrection; Matthew 5 places Jesus' teaching alongside the Law and Prophets; Romans 15 explains how earlier Scripture serves a present community; and Hebrews 1 opens by contrasting earlier prophetic speech with God's speech through the Son. Reading canonically means tracing those stated links and noticing what each author emphasizes, rather than collecting similar phrases as if they proved dependence.
covenantal_significance: Matthew 5:17–20 frames Jesus' relation to the Law and Prophets as fulfillment, while Romans 15:4 and 2 Timothy 3:14–17 describe earlier Scripture as continuing to teach and sustain its readers. A canonical reading therefore asks how continuity and change appear in the texts themselves. It should not assume that every command applies in the same way across every covenant or that later interpretation erases the earlier passage's own setting.

interpretive_notes.note: Read a passage in its own argument and setting first; then follow explicit links that later biblical writers make to it. Luke 24 and Romans 15 offer examples of such links.
Connected reading does not make distinct passages interchangeable. Matthew 5, Romans 15, and Hebrews 1 each describe a different relationship between earlier Scripture and later readers.
